title: The strategic role of the EU fuel manufacturing and refining sector
gist: Oxford Economics (consulting report summary) sizes the EU fuel refining sector at €200bn GDP, 1.8m jobs and €83bn taxes in 2025, and warns a faster-than-expected capacity contraction could cut ~€25bn GDP, ~120,000 jobs and €14bn revenue while raising import reliance by 2035. Only the landing-page summary is available; the full report is gated.

insights.claim: According to Oxford Economics, in 2025 the EU fuel manufacturing and refining sector supported €200 billion in GDP, 1.8 million jobs and €83 billion in tax revenues across the EU.
insights.speaker: Sanele Mjikane
insights.so_what: Quantifies the political weight of EU refining, supporting the case that policymakers will resist rapid capacity loss and may offer support measures.
insights.quote: In 2025, the sector supported €200 billion in GDP, 1.8 million jobs, and €83 billion in tax revenues across the EU

insights.claim: Oxford Economics argues EU refineries remain a strategic pillar of Europe's industrial base because they supply the fuels and feedstocks underpinning transport, manufacturing, petrochemicals, agriculture and household activity.
insights.speaker: Sanele Mjikane
insights.so_what: Refining disruption propagates downstream to petrochemical and industrial users; watch feedstock availability and pricing for EU chemicals.
insights.quote: remains a strategic pillar of Europe’s economy and industrial base
insights.locator: The EU fuel manufacturing and refining industry

themes.theme: Downside scenario from faster capacity contraction

insights.claim: Oxford Economics estimates a faster-than-expected contraction of EU refining capacity could reduce EU GDP by almost €25 billion, eliminate around 120,000 jobs and lower government revenues by €14 billion by 2035.
insights.speaker: Sanele Mjikane
insights.so_what: Scenario framing for lobbying on EU climate/fuel policy; refinery closures announcements are a watch item for EU macro and regional labour markets.
insights.quote: A faster-than-expected contraction could reduce EU GDP by almost €25 billion, eliminate around 120,000 jobs, lower government revenues by €14 billion

insights.claim: Oxford Economics warns that declining EU refining capacity would increase the EU's reliance on imported fuels by 2035, with implications for competitiveness and energy security.
insights.speaker: Sanele Mjikane
insights.so_what: Rising EU product import dependence supports refined-product cracks and seaborne product trade flows into Europe (e.g., diesel/jet imports).
insights.quote: increase the EU’s reliance on imported fuels by 2035, with implications for competitiveness, energy security, and the transition to low-carbon fuels

themes.theme: Refining as enabler of the low-carbon transition

insights.claim: Oxford Economics frames the key risk as EU refining capacity contracting faster than the energy transition can be delivered, arguing the sector has a role in enabling industrial transformation and low-carbon fuels.
insights.speaker: Sanele Mjikane
insights.so_what: Sequencing risk: premature closures could leave Europe short of both fossil and transition fuels; favours policy support for refinery conversion (e.g., low-carbon fuel projects).
insights.quote: the economic risks that could emerge if refining capacity contracts faster than the transition can be delivered
